Such, then, is their position. We, however, shall show what we proposed: the Father did not take “from whom” as his own and then throw “through whom” to the Son; nor again does the Son refuse the Holy Spirit participation in “from whom” and “through whom,” according to the legislation of their new distribution.

“One God and Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” These expressions do not legislate a rule; they distinguish the hypostases. The Apostle did not write in this way to introduce alienation of nature, but to display the union of Father and Son without confusion.

That the expressions are not opposed to one another, and do not stand like battle lines fighting against the natures to which they are applied, is clear from another passage. Blessed Paul brings both expressions together upon one and the same subject when he says: “From him and through him and to him are all things.”

Anyone who pays even a little attention to the meaning may say that this refers plainly to the Lord. The Apostle first places before us the prophecy of Isaiah: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who became his counselor?” and then adds, “For from him and through him and to him are all things.”

That the prophet spoke these things concerning God the Word, the Creator of every creature, may be learned from the preceding words: “Who measured the water in his hand, and the heaven with a span, and all the earth in a handful? Who set the mountains in a balance and the valleys in scales? Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who became his counselor?” Here “who?” does not indicate absolute impossibility, but rarity, as in: “Who will rise up for me against evildoers?” and, “Who is the man who desires life?” and, “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” So here too: “Who knows the mind of the Lord, and who shares his counsel?” For “the Father loves the Son and shows him all things.”

He is the one who holds together the earth and grasps it round about; who brought all things into stability and order; who assigned balance to the mountains, measure to the waters, and its proper order to everything in the world; who encompasses the whole heaven with a small portion of his total power, which the prophetic word figuratively called a span.

Therefore the Apostle appropriately added: “From him and through him and to him are all things.” From him comes to existing things the cause of their being, according to the will of God the Father. Through him all things receive their continuance and constitution, since he created all things and apportions to each created thing what is necessary for its preservation. Therefore all things are turned toward him, looking with irresistible longing and ineffable affection toward the Author and Giver of life, as it is written: “The eyes of all hope in you”; and again, “All things wait upon you”; and, “You open your hand and fill every living thing with good pleasure.”

But if they resist this interpretation, what argument will rescue them from plainly falling into their own trap?

If they refuse to allow that the three expressions—“from him,” “through him,” and “to him”—are spoken of the Lord, they must apply them to God the Father. Then their rule plainly collapses, because not only “from whom” but also “through whom” is found applied to the Father.

If “through whom” contains nothing degrading, why do they reserve it for the Son as though it signified inferiority? But if it necessarily indicates service, let them answer us: under what superior is the God of glory and Father of Christ serving?

Thus they are overturned by their own argument, while our position remains secure whichever way the passage is read. If the passage is about the Son, then “from whom” is found to apply to the Son. If someone insists on referring the prophetic words to God the Father, then he must grant that “through whom” is appropriate to God. The two expressions will possess equal dignity because both are used with equal force of God. In either case, applied to one and the same person, they are shown to be equal in honor.

But let us return to the matter before us.

Writing to the Ephesians, the Apostle says: “Speaking the truth in love, let us grow in every way into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together through every supporting joint, according to the working in the measure of each individual part, makes the growth of the body.”

Again, to the Colossians, concerning those who do not possess knowledge of the Only-begotten, it is said of the one “holding fast to the head,” that is, Christ, “from whom the whole body, supplied through the joints and ligaments, grows with the growth of God.”

That Christ is the head of the Church we have learned elsewhere from the Apostle saying, “He gave him as head over all things to the Church,” and, “From his fullness we all received.” The Lord himself also says of the Spirit, “He will receive from what is mine and declare it to you.”

In general, anyone who searches diligently will find many forms of the expression “from whom.” The Lord himself says, “I knew that power had gone out from me.” Likewise we have observed “from” used many times concerning the Spirit: “The one who sows into the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit”; and John says, “By this we know that he is in us, from the Spirit whom he gave us”; and the angel says, “What has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.” The Lord also says, “What is born from the Spirit is spirit.”

So much for this expression.

We must now show that Scripture accepts the expression “through whom” alike of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

It would be unnecessary to bring testimonies concerning the Son, both because the usage is well known and because our opponents themselves rely upon it. But we show that “through whom” is also used of the Father: “God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son”; and, “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God”; and again, “So you are no longer a slave but a son; and if a son, then an heir through God”; and, “Just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father.” Isaiah too says, “Woe to those who make deep counsel, and not through the Lord.”

Many testimonies may likewise be set out where this expression is applied to the Spirit: “God revealed it to us through the Spirit”; and elsewhere, “Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit”; and again, “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom.”

We can say the same concerning the expression “in”: Scripture has handed down its use also of God the Father.

In the Old Testament it says, “In God we shall do mighty deeds”; “In you is my praise continually”; and again, “In your name I shall rejoice.” Paul says, “In God who created all things”; and, “Paul and Silvanus and Timothy to the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father”; and, “If somehow I may at last be prospered in the will of God to come to you”; and, “You boast in God.” There are more examples than are easy to count.

Our purpose is not to display a great quantity of testimonies, but to refute the uselessness of their rules. Since the use of this expression concerning the Lord and the Holy Spirit is already familiar, we may pass over demonstrating it.

It is also necessary to say that a very strong refutation of those who reject our teaching arises from the contrary conclusion. If, according to their argument, difference of expression proves difference of nature, then identity of expressions now compels them to confess identity without variation of essence.

The uses of these expressions are interchanged not only in theology. They often exchange the meanings normally signified by one another, when one expression takes up the sense of another.

For example, “I have acquired a man through God” means the same as “from God.” Elsewhere Scripture speaks of “all that Moses commanded Israel through the commandment of the Lord.” Again Joseph, speaking to those in prison about their dreams, says, “Is not their interpretation through God?” plainly using “through God” with the sense “from God.”

Conversely, Paul uses “from whom” where one might expect “through whom,” as when he says Christ was “born from a woman.” Elsewhere he clearly distinguishes the normal expressions, attributing to the woman birth “from the man” and to the man birth “through the woman”: “As the woman is from the man, so the man is through the woman.”

Yet here, while at once showing that usage can vary and correcting in passing the error of those who mishandle these expressions, he deliberately uses the stronger phrase concerning the Lord's body in order to show that the God-bearing flesh was truly gathered from the human substance.

For “through a woman” might have suggested merely a passage or channel of birth, whereas “from the woman” sufficiently shows the real communion of nature of the one born.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek text in PG 32.
The chapter is Basil's sustained demonstration that prepositions cannot be rigidly assigned to distinct divine natures.
ὑπόστασις is retained conceptually as 'hypostasis' in the note to section 7; the translation renders the surrounding sentence in ordinary English.
The final discussion of Gal 4:4 is Christological: Basil uses 'from a woman' to insist on the reality of Christ's human flesh.
